# Incident Report — MTA 2024-11-26 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim Host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.11.26.183** | Source of all suspicious traffic; consistent across DNS, SMB, HTTP, TLS |
| MAC | **d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b** | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==10.11.26.183`) and Ethernet source on all frames from .183 |
| Hostname | **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** (workgroup/computer name **NEMOTODES**) | NBNS name query responses; DNS PTR queries for `DESKTOP-B8TQK49` / `DESKTOP-B8TQK49.local` |
| Logged-in user | **oboomwald** | Kerberos `CNameString` field in AS-REQ/TGS traffic to the domain controller |
| AD domain / DC | `nemotoads.health`, DC = **NEMOTODES-DC** at 10.11.26.3 (MAC 00:24:e8:7f:09:5d) | DNS SRV lookups for `_ldap._tcp...nemotoads.health`, NBNS `NEMOTODE-DC` |

## Malware Family: **NetSupport RAT**
**Attribution: signature-confirmed.** Both Suricata/ET signatures and raw application-layer protocol strings agree:
- Suricata alerts: `ETPRO TROJAN NetSupport RAT CnC Activity`, `ETPRO TROJAN Malicious NetSupport Rat CnC Checkin`, `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Checkin`, `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Response`, `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`, `ET POLICY HTTP POST on unusual Port Possibly Hostile`.
- Raw traffic (TCP stream 140/77, `tshark -z follow,tcp,ascii`) shows literal NetSupport client/gateway protocol handshake:
  ```
  POST http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm HTTP/1.1
  User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3
  ...
  CMD=POLL
  INFO=1
  ACK=1

  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  Server: NetSupport Gateway/1.8 (Windows NT)
  CMD=ENCD
  ES=1
  DATA=<encrypted binary blob>
  ```
  This is the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-control protocol (`CMD=POLL/ENCD`), confirming the RAT is a trojanized/abused NetSupport client, not just a heuristic match.

## Infection Timeline (all times relative to alert log, 2024-11-26)
1. **04:49:38** — Baseline noise: `www.msftconnecttest.com` check, burst of NXDOMAIN DNS responses.
2. **04:49:41** — TLS 1.0 session to 4.149.227.78 (benign/unrelated, flagged only for weak TLS version).
3. **04:49:55–04:50:10** — Normal AD/SMB chatter with the DC (10.11.26.3) triggers generic SMBv1/EFSRPC signatures; no evidence this is a lateral-movement exploit, this is routine Windows domain traffic on the host's own DC.
4. **04:50:14** — DNS lookup for **modandcrackedapk.com** (ET CURRENT_EVENTS "ZPHP Domain" — known cracked-software/keygen lure category).
5. **~04:50:11–04:50:26 (t≈33–37s)** — Large TLS session to **classicgrand.com** (213.246.109.5), ~3.4 MB transferred — precedes and likely gates the crack-site visit (redirect/ad-gate in the delivery chain). Not independently signature-flagged, so this indicator is **behavioral**.
6. **04:50:40** — TLS handshake with SNI **modandcrackedapk.com** to 193.42.38.139 — an ~11 MB encrypted session (largest conversation in the capture), consistent with the payload/installer download riding inside TLS.
7. **04:50:45** — Host begins polling **194.180.191.64:443** over plaintext HTTP (port 443 used for HTTP, not TLS — itself an ET POLICY alert) with `fakeurl.htm` NetSupport C2 checkins; sustained POLL/ENCD beaconing continues for the rest of the capture (last seen frame ~26913, session duration ~3164s).
8. **04:50:45** — Host queries `geo.netsupportsoftware.com` (104.26.1.231) `/location/loca.asp` — a NetSupport-brand IP-geolocation lookup, consistent with genuine NetSupport client startup behavior, corroborating the C2 identification.

## Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | **194.180.191.64:443** (HTTP, not TLS, over port 443) | Sustained `POST /fakeurl.htm` POLL/ENCD beacon traffic, `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3`, `Server: NetSupport Gateway/1.8`; ETPRO TROJAN alerts |
| URL | `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` | C2 check-in endpoint, confirmed in HTTP request list and stream follow |
| Domain | **modandcrackedapk.com** (resolves to 193.42.38.139) | DNS A record lookup + TLS SNI; ET CURRENT_EVENTS ZPHP alert; likely initial lure/delivery site |
| Domain | **classicgrand.com** (resolves to 213.246.109.5) | TLS SNI, large (3.4 MB) session immediately preceding the modandcrackedapk.com visit — behavioral indicator (redirect/ad-gate), not independently signature-confirmed |
| Domain (RAT infra) | **geo.netsupportsoftware.com** (104.26.1.231) | HTTP GET `/location/loca.asp`, ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup alert |
| File name / hash | **None recoverable** | The only payload-sized transfer (modandcrackedapk.com, ~11 MB) is fully TLS-encrypted end to end; no plaintext HTTP object matching an executable/installer was observed. `--export-objects http` over the full capture yields only benign OS/browser objects (Windows Update CABs, OCSP response, connecttest.txt, Adobe ProcessMAU.txt, NetSupport fakeurl.htm/loca.asp) — none are the malware binary itself. |

## Benign / Noise Context (do not treat as IOCs)
- `www.msftconnecttest.com`, `dns.msftncsi.com` — Windows NCSI connectivity checks.
- Extensive Microsoft/Office 365/Bing/MSN telemetry and CDN traffic (`*.resources.office.net`, `login.live.com`, `windowsupdate.com`, `smartscreen.microsoft.com`, etc.).
- `r10.o.lencr.org` — Let's Encrypt OCSP.
- `acroipm2.adobe.com/.../ProcessMAU.txt` — Adobe Acrobat update-check telemetry.
- SMBv1/EFSRPC/NTLMSSP alerts against the host's own domain controller (10.11.26.3) — routine authenticated AD traffic mis-flagged by generic exploit signatures, no corroborating evidence of an actual overflow/exploit.
- TLS 1.0 session to 4.149.227.78 — flagged only for using an outdated TLS version, no other malicious indicator tied to it.

## Summary
Windows workstation **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** (10.11.26.183, MAC d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b), logged in as domain user **oboomwald** on the `nemotoads.health` AD domain, was infected with **NetSupport RAT** (attribution signature-confirmed via both Suricata ETPRO rules and raw NetSupport client/gateway protocol strings). The infection chain began with DNS/TLS activity to a redirect domain (**classicgrand.com**) and a cracked-software lure domain (**modandcrackedapk.com**, TLS-encrypted ~11 MB download), after which the host began persistent HTTP-over-443 beaconing to the C2 at **194.180.191.64:443** (`/fakeurl.htm`, POLL/ENCD protocol) that continued for the remainder of the capture. No plaintext malware binary or hash could be recovered because the delivery session was fully TLS-encrypted.
